reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly assumes horizontal acceleration exists in projectile motion.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: In projectile motion without air resistance, there is no horizontal force, so horizontal acceleration is zero. Horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

miniLesson.explain: In projectile motion, horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Vertically, gravity causes constant downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s². Horizontally, there is no force (ignoring air resistance), so acceleration is zero. This means horizontal velocity never changes.
miniLesson.example: Consider a bean bag thrown horizontally from a height. It lands after 1.43 s, and the horizontal displacement is 4.3 m. The horizontal speed is constant (4.3 m / 1.43 s = 3.0 m/s) throughout the flight. It does not speed up or slow down horizontally.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Imagine a puck on an air hockey table – it slides at constant speed. In projectile motion, the horizontal motion is just like that: no acceleration horizontally.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the horizontal acceleration of a projectile in the absence of air resistance?
A projectile is launched horizontally. Its flight time is 1.43 s and it lands 4.3 m away. What is the horizontal acceleration during its flight?
guidedPractice.answer: 0 m/s². (Horizontal acceleration is always zero in projectile motion without air resistance.)

guidedPractice.prompt: A soccer ball is kicked at an angle of 40° with an initial speed of 9.4 m/s. At the highest point of its trajectory, what is the horizontal acceleration?
guidedPractice.answer: 0 m/s². (Horizontal acceleration is zero at all times, including at the top, because no horizontal force acts.)

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly states that vertical acceleration is zero at maximum height.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks that because vertical velocity is momentarily zero at the apex, the acceleration must also be zero. In reality, acceleration due to gravity is constant at 9.8 m/s² downward throughout the flight.

miniLesson.explain: In projectile motion, the vertical acceleration is always 9.8 m/s² downward, regardless of the object's position. At the maximum height, the vertical velocity is zero, but the acceleration remains constant. This is because gravity is a continuous force. Even at the top, the ball is still being pulled downward, which is why it begins to descend.
miniLesson.example: Consider a soccer ball kicked at 40° with speed 9.4 m/s. It reaches a maximum height of 2.12 m. At that instant, its vertical velocity is 0 m/s, but its vertical acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downward. This constant acceleration causes the ball to then accelerate downward.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Gravity never takes a break – it always pulls down at 9.8 m/s², even at the top.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: At the highest point of a projectile's flight, the vertical acceleration is 0 m/s².
guidedPractice.answer: False. The vertical acceleration is always 9.8 m/s² downward.

guidedPractice.prompt: A ball is launched from ground at an angle. At its maximum height, what is the value of vertical acceleration?
Explain why a projectile's vertical acceleration is constant even when its vertical velocity is zero. Use a specific example from class (e.g., a ball reaching max height in 0.37 s).
guidedPractice.answer: Gravity acts continuously. At the top, vertical velocity is zero but acceleration due to gravity is still 9.8 m/s² downward. For example, in class we saw a ball that reached its maximum height in 0.37 s; during that entire time, its vertical acceleration was constant at 9.8 m/s² down, which is why it eventually reversed direction.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect option in diagnostic question diag-sph3u-proj-q3, using sine for horizontal component or cosine for vertical component.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses the trigonometric functions for component decomposition, thinking that horizontal component is v sinθ and vertical is v cosθ.

miniLesson.explain: When launching a projectile at an angle θ above horizontal, the initial velocity v is split into horizontal and vertical components. The horizontal component is along the x-axis (adjacent to the angle) so it uses cosine: v_x = v cosθ. The vertical component is along the y-axis (opposite to the angle) so it uses sine: v_y = v sinθ. Remember: x = adjacent = cos, y = opposite = sin.
miniLesson.example: A soccer ball is launched at 40° with speed 9.4 m/s. Using cos40° ≈ 0.766 and sin40° ≈ 0.643, we get v_x = 9.4 × 0.766 ≈ 7.2 m/s and v_y = 9.4 × 0.643 ≈ 6.0 m/s.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think 'x is cos, y is sin' — horizontal uses cosine, vertical uses sine.

guidedPractice.prompt: A projectile is launched at an angle. Which trigonometric function do you use to find the horizontal component?
A soccer ball is kicked with speed 9.4 m/s at 40° above horizontal. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of initial velocity.
guidedPractice.answer: Horizontal = 9.4 × cos40° ≈ 7.2 m/s, Vertical = 9.4 × sin40° ≈ 6.0 m/s

guidedPractice.prompt: A golf ball is launched from a cliff at 50° above horizontal. Its initial vertical component is 12.5 m/s. What is the launch speed? (Use sin50° ≈ 0.766)

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers total flight time equals time to maximum height instead of doubling it.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks that the time to reach maximum height is the total flight time, failing to account for the symmetric descent.

miniLesson.explain: For a projectile that launches from and lands at the same height (symmetric launch), the upward and downward parts of the flight are mirror images. Because vertical acceleration is constant (9.8 m/s² downward), the time to slow to zero at the top equals the time to accelerate back down to the launch speed. Therefore, total flight time = 2 × time to maximum height.
miniLesson.example: In the soccer ball example from class (launched at 40° with speed 9.4 m/s), the total flight time was 1.3 s. Since it lands at the same height, the time to reach maximum height is exactly half: 0.65 s.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: What goes up must come down in the same time – symmetrical!

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the relationship between the time to maximum height and total flight time for a symmetric projectile launch?
guidedPractice.answer: Total flight time = 2 × time to maximum height.

guidedPractice.prompt: A ball is launched from ground level and lands at the same height. Its time to maximum height is 0.37 s. What is the total flight time?
In the soccer ball example, the total flight time was 1.3 s. Explain why the time to maximum height is half of that, and calculate it.
guidedPractice.answer: Because the launch and landing heights are equal, the upward and downward motions are symmetric. So time to max height = total flight time / 2 = 1.3 s / 2 = 0.65 s.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched horizontally from a cliff. Which of the following best describes its horizontal acceleration during the entire flight (ignoring air resistance)?
Explain why the horizontal acceleration of any projectile (ignoring air resistance) is always zero, even when the projectile is launched at an angle.
questions.rubric: Student must state that no horizontal force acts (gravity only acts vertically), so horizontal acceleration is zero. Also mention that horizontal velocity remains constant.

questions.stem: A cannonball is fired at an angle. At the highest point of its path, which of the following is true about its vertical acceleration?
options: It depends on the launch speed.

questions.stem: A baseball is thrown upward and reaches its maximum height. Explain why the vertical acceleration at that point is not zero, even though its vertical velocity is momentarily zero.
questions.rubric: Student correctly states that acceleration due to gravity is always 9.8 m/s² downward, regardless of velocity. They explain that gravity is a constant force causing the ball to decelerate upward and accelerate downward, so at the top it is still experiencing 9.8 m/s² downward, which is why it begins to fall. Mention of continuous force or constant gravitational acceleration is expected.

questions.stem: For a projectile launched at an angle θ above horizontal, which expression gives the horizontal component of the initial velocity?
A soccer ball is launched at 40° above horizontal with a speed of 9.4 m/s. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity. Round each to one decimal place.
questions.rubric: Horizontal component = 9.4 × cos40° ≈ 7.2 m/s (accept 7.1-7.3). Vertical component = 9.4 × sin40° ≈ 6.0 m/s (accept 5.9-6.1). Both values must be correct with appropriate units (m/s) and correct trigonometric function use.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched from a cliff and lands on the ground below. The time to reach maximum height is 0.37 s. Which of the following is true about the total flight time?
Explain why the total flight time for a projectile launched from ground level and landing at the same height is exactly twice the time to maximum height.
questions.rubric: Student explains that for same launch and landing height, the vertical motion is symmetric: time to go up equals time to go down because acceleration is constant. (1 point) States that total time is sum of up and down times, so total = 2 * time up. (1 point) Provides a correct explanation using kinematics or symmetry. (1 point) Max 3 points. Pass: at least 2 points.

retestCards.passRule: Question 1 correct and Question 2 achieves at least 2 out of 3 rubric points.
